endorsements.quote: Clinically, the roadmap should be staged to ensure safe and incremental adoption (Fig. 3c ).
As such, automation bias must be treated as a first-class design constraint, rather than a downstream deployment risk.

In this framework, the agent’s capabilities are intentionally restricted in Phase I for example, operating offline or under tight clinician supervision with progressive expansion of autonomy and integration across Phases II–IV as evidence accumulates.

Additionally, clear guidelines defining accountability and liability are needed to determine the respective responsibilities of AI developers, healthcare institutions, and clinicians in cases of adverse outcomes.
The ultimate decision-making authority, however, must remain firmly in the hands of human clinicians to preserve the nuance and contextual judgment central to psychiatric care.
Mitigation requires not only explainable AI interfaces but also formal training programs that teach clinicians to question and contextualize AI suggestions.

Equity and generalizability should be reported across demographic and clinical subgroups (including severity), alongside robustness and longitudinal validity (calibration, stability under distribution shift, drift monitoring and governance in post-deployment use).
Yet such monitoring systems risk generating false positives that could lead to unnecessary interventions or patient anxiety.

For any system that interacts with patients, it is also essential to measure escalation behavior and safety overrides, that is how reliably the system routes high-risk situations to human care and what happens after escalation rather than assuming safe behavior from design alone.
Prioritizing diverse, representative training data is essential to reduce the perpetuation of existing systemic disparities.

Transparent governance mechanisms, including oversight bodies with clearly defined accountability structures, are necessary to establish responsibility when AI systems influence diagnostic or therapeutic pathways 40 – 42 .
Long-term expenses include data curation, audit logging, model monitoring, retraining, governance committees, and user support, all of which must be budgeted as part of implementation.

unlisted_practices: Conduct routine bias audits evaluating model performance across demographic subgroups.
Ensure patients understand when they are interacting with AI rather than a clinician.
Evaluate patient usability, acceptability, adherence, and therapeutic alliance as core endpoints in trials of AI systems.
Obtain ongoing, reversible patient consent for continuous monitoring, supported by transparent data-use policies.
Conduct health-economic and cost-effectiveness evaluation before scaling up AI deployment.
Use co-design with clinicians, patients, and lived-experience advisory panels throughout AI development and deployment.
Use privacy-preserving techniques such as federated learning and differential privacy while accounting for their accuracy trade-offs.
Pilot AI systems in regulatory sandbox environments and develop adaptive regulatory frameworks.
Monitor for concept and covariate drift and integrate drift detection alerts into deployment pipelines.

screen.reason: This is a perspective piece outlining definitions, roles, and a roadmap for responsible implementation of agentic AI in psychiatry.
